note: Written September 2026. Fares checked against the MTA: the subway and bus base fare rose to $3.00 in January 2026, OMNY caps a week of rides at $35, and the unlimited MetroCard passes have been retired. Restaurants and opening arrangements change, so confirm before you go.

glance.why: New York is a walking city disguised as a skyline. The famous sights are mostly worth doing once and quickly; what the city actually rewards is covering ground on foot, block by block, between neighbourhoods that change character in a hundred metres. Manhattan below 59th Street and the western edge of Brooklyn will hold a first visit comfortably, and the single best decision a visitor makes is to spend less time in observation decks and more time eating, walking and going to something - a show, a game, a gig, a museum with one exhibition you actually want to see.
glance.idealStay: 4-5 days for a first visit; 6-7 to include outer-borough neighbourhoods and a slower pace

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, with a plan and a time limit
The Brooklyn Bridge walked toward Manhattan at dusk
The 9/11 Memorial and the harbour from the Staten Island Ferry
Greenwich Village and the West Village on foot
One meal each in Chinatown, a deli, and a neighbourhood in another borough

history.story: New York was Lenape land, then a Dutch trading post called New Amsterdam in 1624, taken by the English forty years later and renamed. Its harbour made it the continent's port, the Erie Canal in 1825 made it the outlet for a continent's goods, and immigration made it the country's largest city - German and Irish first, then Italian, Eastern European Jewish, and after 1965 Caribbean, Latin American, Chinese, South Asian and West African. The consolidation of the five boroughs in 1898, the elevator and the steel frame, the subway in 1904, the Great Migration and the Harlem Renaissance, the postwar boom, the near-bankruptcy and crime of the 1970s and 80s, gentrification, September 11 and the pandemic are all still legible in specific streets.
history.origins: The deep, protected harbour at the mouth of the Hudson is the whole reason for the city. Manhattan's hard schist bedrock is why the towers could be built where they were, and the 1811 grid above Houston Street is why navigating uptown is trivial and downtown is not.

periods.name: Lenapehoking and New Amsterdam, to 1664
periods.text: Lenape land becomes a Dutch trading company outpost; the street pattern of the Financial District still follows it.

periods.name: Port city, 1825-1890
periods.text: The Erie Canal makes New York the country's commercial gateway; tenement districts fill with new arrivals.

periods.name: Immigrant city, 1880-1924
periods.text: Ellis Island, the Lower East Side tenements, and the political machines and labour movements that came with them.

periods.name: Skyscraper city, 1900-1940
periods.text: The subway, the Woolworth, Chrysler and Empire State buildings, and Rockefeller Center define the skyline and the idea of the city.

periods.name: Harlem Renaissance and the Great Migration
periods.text: Black American life and culture reshape uptown and, through it, American music and letters.

periods.name: Crisis and reinvention, 1970s-
periods.text: Fiscal collapse, crime, AIDS and the artistic explosion that accompanied them; then the safer, richer and more expensive city that followed, and the long recovery from September 11.

history.whyItMatters: New York's history is mostly domestic rather than monumental - it is in tenement stairwells, subway tile, brownstone stoops and the shopfronts of businesses that outlived their neighbourhoods. That is why the Tenement Museum tells the city's story better than most of its grander institutions.
visible: Dutch and colonial: the crooked streets of the Financial District, Fraunces Tavern, Trinity Church
Immigrant New York: the Lower East Side tenements, the Tenement Museum, Ellis Island
Gilded Age: the Met, Grand Central Terminal, Fifth Avenue mansions turned museums
Skyscraper era: the Chrysler and Empire State buildings, Rockefeller Center, the Woolworth Building
Modern city: the High Line, Hudson Yards, the 9/11 Memorial and Museum

historic.name: Brooklyn Bridge
historic.why: Walk it toward Manhattan, late afternoon, and continue into Dumbo or the Financial District. Free, and the best thirty minutes in the city.

historic.name: 9/11 Memorial and Museum
historic.why: The memorial pools are free and quietly devastating; the museum is thorough and heavy, so allow time and headspace.

historic.name: Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island
historic.why: The Ellis Island immigration museum is the substantive half. If time is short, the free Staten Island Ferry passes the statue instead.

historic.name: Grand Central Terminal
historic.why: Ten minutes for the concourse ceiling, longer if you eat downstairs. A working building, not an attraction.

historic.name: Tenement Museum
historic.why: Guided tours through restored apartments of actual families; the best single hour of history in New York.

historic.name: Empire State Building or Top of the Rock
historic.why: Choose one. Top of the Rock puts the Empire State in your photo; the Empire State puts you in the more famous building.

arts.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
arts.why: Too big to see. Pick three departments - Egyptian, European painting, the American Wing, Arms and Armor - and leave before you are exhausted.

arts.name: Museum of Modern Art
arts.why: The best modern collection in the world and a building designed to move crowds through it. Go at opening or on a late evening.

arts.name: American Museum of Natural History
arts.why: The dioramas, the blue whale and the Gilder Center; the most rewarding museum in the city for children.

arts.name: The Frick Collection
arts.why: A Gilded Age mansion full of masterpieces, reopened in 2025 after a long renovation; small enough to finish in one visit.

arts.name: Whitney Museum of American Art
arts.why: American art in a Renzo Piano building with terraces over the High Line.

arts.name: The Met Cloisters
arts.why: Medieval art in a reassembled monastery above the Hudson. Worth the subway ride for the quiet alone.

nature.name: Central Park
nature.why: Enter at 59th and walk north to the Ramble and the Reservoir rather than doing a loop of the south end with everyone else.

nature.name: The High Line
nature.why: An elevated rail viaduct turned park; twenty blocks, crowded at midday, best early or at dusk.

nature.name: Brooklyn Bridge Park
nature.why: The best skyline view in the city, plus a carousel, piers and the Promenade above it.

nature.name: Prospect Park
nature.why: The same designers as Central Park, with better meadows and fewer visitors. Pair with the Botanic Garden.

nature.name: Staten Island Ferry
nature.why: Free, twenty-five minutes each way, passes the Statue of Liberty. The best-value thing in New York.

nature.name: Governors Island
nature.why: A car-free island with hammocks, hills and skyline views; seasonal ferry from Lower Manhattan.

shopping.name: SoHo
shopping.why: Flagships and boutiques under cast iron; the buildings are as good as the shops.

shopping.name: Fifth Avenue and Midtown
shopping.why: Department stores and flagship spectacle; efficient if you want it, skippable if you do not.

shopping.name: Lower East Side and Nolita
shopping.why: Independent designers, vintage, and small shops that still feel like the owner is inside.

shopping.name: Chelsea Market
shopping.why: Food hall in a former Nabisco factory at the foot of the High Line; busy but useful.

shopping.name: Brooklyn Flea and Smorgasburg
shopping.why: Weekend markets for vintage and street food; check the season and location before going.

shopping.name: Strand and the bookshops
shopping.why: Eighteen miles of books, plus McNally Jackson and the small shops downtown.

nightlife.name: Broadway and off-Broadway
nightlife.why: The reason many people come. Off-Broadway is cheaper, often better, and easier to book.

nightlife.name: Jazz in the West Village
nightlife.why: The Village Vanguard, Smalls and Blue Note within a few blocks; the Vanguard is the one to book.

nightlife.name: Lower East Side bars
nightlife.why: The densest run of bars downtown, from dives to cocktail rooms with no sign.

nightlife.name: Brooklyn live music
nightlife.why: Warehouse venues and small rooms; where most of the interesting bookings are.

nightlife.name: Comedy clubs
nightlife.why: The Comedy Cellar and its neighbours run several shows a night with famous drop-ins.

nightlife.name: A game at the Garden or the ballpark
nightlife.why: Knicks or Rangers at Madison Square Garden, Yankees or Mets in summer; the crowd is the event.

food.identity: New York's food identity is immigration plus competition. The city has no cuisine of its own beyond a handful of forms it perfected - the bagel and appetising counter, the pastrami sandwich, the coal-oven and then the by-the-slice pizza, the Cantonese-American dining room, the diner - and beyond those it simply has the best version of almost everything, somewhere, usually far from Midtown. The instinct that ruins visits is eating near the sights. The instinct that saves them is picking a neighbourhood, taking the subway there and eating what it is known for: Sichuan in Flushing, Colombian and Indian in Jackson Heights, Middle Eastern in Bay Ridge, Dominican in Washington Heights.

mustTry.dish: A bagel with lox and cream cheese
mustTry.what: Boiled-then-baked bagel, sliced salmon, cream cheese, from an appetising shop or a corner bagel counter.
mustTry.why: The most specifically New York breakfast there is, from the city's Eastern European Jewish history.
mustTry.flavour: Chewy, salty, cold and rich all at once.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Standing up, in the morning, ordered fast and precisely.

mustTry.what: Hand-cut cured and smoked beef, piled on rye with mustard, at a Jewish deli.
mustTry.why: One of the few dishes the city genuinely invented and still does better than anywhere.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Split it, and never ask for mayonnaise.

mustTry.what: A plain slice from a counter, and a coal- or wood-oven pie from a sit-down place.
mustTry.why: The slice is daily life; the pie is the craft version.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Folded lengthwise, standing at the counter.

mustTry.what: Soup dumplings, hand-pulled noodles and roast meats in Manhattan's Chinatown, Sunset Park or Flushing.
mustTry.why: New York's Chinese food is regionally deep in a way few western cities match.
mustTry.flavour: Varies wildly by region - go where the menu is specific.

mustTry.what: Chicken and rice with white sauce and hot sauce, from a street cart.
mustTry.why: The city's default late-night and lunch-hour meal.

mustTry.what: Eggs, home fries, endless filter coffee in a booth.
mustTry.why: A vanishing but still-living form, and the cheapest sit-down meal in Manhattan.

mustTry.what: East Coast oysters at a raw bar, with something cold and dry.
mustTry.why: The city was built on oyster beds, and the raw bar remains one of its best rooms.

mustTry.what: Colombian arepas, Tibetan momos, Indian sweets, Mexican tacos - often on one block in Jackson Heights.
mustTry.why: The most diverse eating in the United States, and mostly under fifteen dollars.

mustTry.what: Dense baked cheesecake, and the flat iced cookie every deli sells.
mustTry.why: The city's two classic sweets, both better than their reputations.

mustTry.what: The city's fine dining, from Le Bernardin's seafood to smaller counters downtown.
mustTry.why: New York's high end is genuinely world-class if the budget allows one.

iconic.name: Katz's Delicatessen
iconic.desc: A cafeteria-system deli that has been carving pastrami since 1888.
iconic.dishes: Pastrami on rye, matzo ball soup
iconic.whyGo: The single most recognisable meal in New York, and it lives up to it.
iconic.booking: No; take a ticket and hold onto it

iconic.name: Russ & Daughters
iconic.desc: A century-old smoked-fish counter, with a sit-down cafe around the corner.
iconic.dishes: Lox, sturgeon, whitefish salad on a bagel
iconic.whyGo: The best short lesson in Jewish New York available.
iconic.booking: Counter is walk-in; the cafe takes bookings

iconic.name: Grand Central Oyster Bar
iconic.desc: Vaulted tile ceilings under the station, open since 1913.
iconic.dishes: Oysters at the counter, pan roast
iconic.whyGo: A great room and a genuinely good raw bar in the middle of Midtown.

bestFood.name: Le Bernardin
bestFood.desc: Decades at the top of the city's fine dining, built entirely on fish.
bestFood.whyGo: If you spend once, spend here.

bestFood.name: Via Carota
bestFood.desc: A small room doing vegetables and pasta better than places charging three times as much.
bestFood.dishes: Insalata verde, cacio e pepe, the roast
bestFood.whyGo: The best neighbourhood restaurant in Manhattan.

bestFood.name: Xi'an Famous Foods
bestFood.desc: Hand-ripped noodles and cumin lamb from a chain that started in a Flushing basement.
bestFood.whyGo: Fifteen dollars for one of the most distinctive meals in the city.

bestValue.name: Joe's Pizza
bestValue.desc: A counter, a slice, and nowhere to sit.
bestValue.whyGo: The New York slice at its most correct.

bestValue.name: Jackson Heights food streets
bestValue.desc: Roosevelt Avenue and the blocks around it: momos, arepas, tacos, sweets.
bestValue.dishes: Whatever the longest queue is for
bestValue.whyGo: The most interesting cheap eating in the country.

bestValue.name: Halal carts
bestValue.desc: Chicken and rice from a cart, at almost any hour.

special.name: Le Bernardin
special.whyGo: The safest choice for a once-in-a-trip dinner.

special.name: Gramercy Tavern
special.desc: A warmer kind of fine dining, with a walk-in tavern room at the front.
special.dishes: Tasting menu in the dining room, or the tavern menu at the bar
special.whyGo: New York hospitality at its most polished without being stiff.
special.booking: Dining room needs booking; tavern takes walk-ins

casual.name: A corner diner
casual.desc: Booths, filter coffee refills and a menu with eleven pages.
casual.whyGo: The cheapest sit-down breakfast in Manhattan and a disappearing institution.

casual.name: Chinatown noodle shops
casual.desc: Small rooms doing one thing - noodles, roast meats, dumplings - very well.
casual.dishes: Hand-pulled noodles, roast pork over rice
casual.whyGo: Excellent food for under twenty dollars, minutes from the bridge.

casual.name: Smorgasburg
casual.desc: Weekend outdoor food market on the Brooklyn waterfront and in Prospect Park.

cafes.name: Veniero's or an old Italian pasticceria
cafes.desc: Cannoli, cheesecake and marble counters from the Italian East Village.
cafes.whyGo: A surviving piece of a neighbourhood that has otherwise changed completely.

cafes.name: Devocion or a Brooklyn roaster
cafes.desc: Bright, plant-filled rooms with serious single-origin coffee.
cafes.whyGo: Where the city's coffee scene actually lives.

cafes.name: Levain Bakery

experiences.name: Walk the Brooklyn Bridge at dusk
experiences.what: Start on the Brooklyn side and walk toward the skyline as the lights come on.
experiences.why: Free, twenty minutes, and better than any observation deck.

experiences.name: Ride the Staten Island Ferry
experiences.what: Round trip past the Statue of Liberty, on the deck at the back.
experiences.why: Free, and the harbour is how the city makes sense.

experiences.name: See a show
experiences.what: Broadway, off-Broadway, or a play in a hundred-seat room downtown.
experiences.why: The depth of live performance here is the city's real cultural advantage.

experiences.name: Jazz at the Village Vanguard
experiences.what: A basement room that has run continuously since 1935.
experiences.why: The most storied jazz club in the world, and still a working one.

experiences.name: Eat a neighbourhood in another borough
experiences.what: Flushing, Jackson Heights, Sunset Park, Astoria or Arthur Avenue in the Bronx.
experiences.why: It is where the city actually eats, and the subway makes it easy.

experiences.name: Sunday gospel or live music in Harlem
experiences.what: A church service that welcomes visitors, or a set at a Harlem club.
experiences.why: Harlem's cultural history is a living thing, not a plaque.

experiences.name: A game
experiences.what: Knicks or Rangers at the Garden, Yankees or Mets in summer.
experiences.why: The crowd, the food and the ritual are the point more than the sport.

experiences.name: Gallery hopping in Chelsea
experiences.what: The blocks between 10th and 11th Avenues, free, on a Thursday.
experiences.why: The commercial art world at full volume, and no admission fee.

experiences.name: Cross Central Park on foot
experiences.what: Enter at one corner and come out the other, taking the paths that look wrong.
experiences.why: The park was designed to be wandered, not photographed.

experiences.name: Ride the subway late
experiences.what: Take a train somewhere specific after 10pm.
experiences.why: The city's 24-hour subway is a genuine oddity and the fastest way anywhere.

timeGuidance.three: Day 1 downtown: the Village, the Lower East Side, the Brooklyn Bridge at dusk. Day 2 uptown: Central Park and the Met, with a show at night. Day 3 the harbour and the 9/11 Memorial, then Chelsea and the High Line.
timeGuidance.fivePlus: Add MoMA, a full outer-borough eating day in Queens or Brooklyn, Harlem, a second park - Prospect or Governors Island - and one thing booked in advance that you would not do at home: a game, a gig, a jazz set or an off-Broadway play.

practical.gettingAround: The subway runs 24 hours and is the correct default. Tap a contactless card, phone or watch straight on the OMNY reader - the base fare rose to $3.00 in January 2026, and OMNY caps you at $35 for a week of subway and local bus rides, which replaced the old unlimited MetroCard passes. Buses are slower but useful crosstown. Above Houston Street the grid makes navigation trivial: avenues run north-south, streets east-west, and twenty blocks is roughly a mile. Below it, carry a map. Walking is genuinely the fastest way to cover short distances in Manhattan, taxis and rideshares are slow in Midtown traffic, and the NYC Ferry is a cheap, scenic way to reach Brooklyn and Queens. For the airports, the AirTrain plus subway or rail from JFK and Newark is far cheaper than a car, and about as fast in traffic.
practical.whenToGo: Autumn, September to early November, is the best season: clear, cool and the full cultural calendar. Spring, April to June, is nearly as good, with parks at their best. Summer is hot, humid and can be unpleasant in the subway, but the city empties slightly and the outdoor programme - concerts, films in the parks, rooftops, beaches - is at full strength. Winter is cold and grey, but it is the cheapest season, the museums and theatres are the point, and the two weeks around Christmas are an expensive, crowded spectacle that some people specifically travel for.

howLong.one: Central Park, the Met or MoMA, a walk downtown through the Village, and the Brooklyn Bridge at dusk.
howLong.twoThree: Add the harbour, the Lower East Side, a show and one observation deck. The classic first visit, still rushed.
howLong.fourFive: The right length: two museums, two neighbourhood walking days, an outer borough and something booked in advance.
howLong.week: Add Queens and the Bronx, Prospect Park and Brooklyn's museums, a Hudson Valley day trip and time to repeat what you liked.

culture: Tipping is expected and is not optional: 18-20 per cent in restaurants and bars, a dollar or two per drink at a bar counter.
Sales tax is added at the register, so the shelf price is never the final price.
Walk fast, stand to the right on escalators, and step out of the pedestrian flow before stopping to look at your phone.
Order quickly and specifically at delis, bagel counters and pizza windows; the queue behind you is the reason.
Subway platforms are hot in summer and trains are aggressively air-conditioned; carry a layer.
Most museums have suggested or pay-what-you-wish admission for New York State residents only - visitors pay the full price, so budget accordingly.
Bars and restaurants often ask for ID for anyone buying alcohol, regardless of apparent age; carry a passport or a copy.

whatIdDo.plan: Start downtown: coffee in the West Village, walk Bleecker and the crooked streets to Washington Square, then east into the Lower East Side for the Tenement Museum and lunch at Katz's. Late afternoon over the Brooklyn Bridge into Dumbo for the skyline, dinner in Brooklyn Heights.
Central Park from the south, crossing north through the Ramble to the Reservoir. The Met in the afternoon - three departments only. Early dinner near Lincoln Center, then a show.
The 9/11 Memorial in the morning, then the Staten Island Ferry there and back for the harbour. Afternoon on the High Line and the Chelsea galleries; oysters and a martini somewhere in the evening.
Out to Queens: Jackson Heights or Flushing for a long, cheap, excellent lunch. Back for MoMA in the late afternoon, then jazz in the Village.
Brooklyn: Prospect Park and the Botanic Garden, Williamsburg in the afternoon, an early dinner somewhere you have to book, and one observation deck at sunset if the weather is clear.
